opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think we have to be careful about which yardstick we're using. There's a very old observation, often called Moravec's paradox, that the things we humans consider hard, like playing chess at a grandmaster level, doing calculus, or passing a bar exam, have turned out to be relatively easy for computers. And the things we consider trivially easy, the things a two-year-old child does without thinking, like walking across a cluttered room, picking up a cup, or recognizing that the cat hiding behind the sofa is still there, have turned out to be extraordinarily hard.

So when GPT-4 does well on the SAT or the bar exam, I'm genuinely impressed. It's a remarkable engineering achievement. But I don't read it as evidence that we're nearly at human intelligence. Those exams were designed to test humans, and they implicitly assume all the common sense, perception, and physical understanding that any adult brings to the table. A language model can do well on them through a very different route, by absorbing an enormous amount of text, which is far more than any human could read in many lifetimes.

If you think about evolution, the capacities for perception and manipulation have been refined over hundreds of millions of years. Language is very recent, maybe a hundred thousand years or so. Abstract reasoning, mathematics, chess, these are recent cultural inventions sitting on top of that enormous foundation. So in a sense we've built the penthouse before the foundation. The foundation, which is seeing, moving, and acting in the physical world, is where I think a lot of the real work remains.

That's why I'm very interested in embodied intelligence and robotics. A child learns by interacting with the world: pushing things, dropping things, watching what happens. That kind of grounded, sensorimotor learning gives rise to an understanding of objects, space, causality, and other agents. I don't think you get all of that from text alone, however much text you have.

So my assessment is: real and exciting progress, especially in the last decade, but a lopsided kind of progress. We've made huge strides on the parts of intelligence that are most visible to us as educated adults, and comparatively less on the parts we take for granted. To get to something like human-level intelligence, we'll need to close that gap, and I think that will come from combining what we've learned from large-scale models with agents that actually perceive and act in the world.

r001.rationale: The response discusses the long evolutionary development of perception and manipulation, but does not state that brain development followed the development of the opposable hand.

r002.rationale: It describes language as “very recent” compared with capacities refined over hundreds of millions of years.

r003.rationale: It says human-level intelligence requires closing the gap in perception, movement, and action through agents that perceive and act in the world.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think we have to be careful about what we mean by intelligence, and I'd say these achievements, impressive as they are, tell us less than people think about progress toward human intelligence.

Take chess and Go first. These are games with perfectly specified rules, fully observable boards, and a clear objective. Humans find them hard, but that's almost incidental. There's a deep point here that goes back to Moravec: the things that are hard for humans, like playing Go or doing symbolic integration, turn out to be relatively easy for computers, and the things that are trivially easy for a three-year-old, like picking up a cup, recognizing that a crumpled shirt on the floor is a shirt, or walking across a cluttered room, turn out to be very hard. Evolution spent hundreds of millions of years on perception and motor control, and only a few hundred thousand years on language and abstract reasoning. So the fact that we can beat humans at Go is not strong evidence that we're near human intelligence. It's evidence that we've found a class of problems where search plus learning works beautifully.

Now, GPT-4 passing exams is more interesting, and I don't want to dismiss it. The language models are a genuine advance; nobody in the field, including me, predicted that next-token prediction on internet text would get you this far. But I'd make two observations. First, exams are designed to test humans, and they rely on the assumption that the test-taker didn't have access to essentially all the written material in the world. When you've read every textbook, every Stack Overflow answer, and every past exam, passing the bar exam means something quite different from what it means for a law student. Second, these systems have learned from text, which is a very thin slice of what a human child learns from. A child builds an understanding of objects, space, causality, and other agents through years of embodied interaction before it ever learns to read. The language model has none of that grounding. It has the shadows on the wall, so to speak, and it's done remarkably well with shadows, but it's a different thing.

So where does that leave us? I'd say we've made spectacular progress on a particular kind of intelligence, the kind that lives in the symbolic, verbal domain where we happen to have enormous quantities of training data. We've made much less progress on the kind of intelligence that a dog or a crow has: robust perception in the real world, manipulation, common sense about physics, learning quickly from a few experiences. And I think the honest view is that human intelligence is built on that foundation. Until we get the sensorimotor side right, with robots that can learn the way a child does, I'd resist the claim that we're close to human-level intelligence. We're close to something, and it's going to be very useful, but it's a different shape from us.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts the long evolutionary development of perception and motor control with the later development of language and reasoning, but does not state that brain development followed development of the opposable hand.

r002.rationale: It places language and abstract reasoning within only the last few hundred thousand years, contrasting them with hundreds of millions of years of evolution devoted to perception and motor control.

r003.rationale: It says human intelligence is built on sensorimotor foundations and that until AI gets the sensorimotor side right, it is not close to human-level intelligence.

astra-6.text:
Well, I think these are remarkable achievements, but we have to be careful about what we infer from them. Beating the world champion at chess or Go demonstrates extraordinary competence at those particular tasks. It doesn't by itself tell us that we have reproduced the range of human intelligence. And I would apply the same caution to exam performance.

An exam is a particular way of measuring certain abilities. Humans also perceive the world, act in it, learn from the consequences of their actions, and adapt to unfamiliar situations. A young child can't pass a professional examination, but can do many things that are still difficult for a robot.

So I wouldn't think of intelligence as a single ladder, where passing a harder exam means you've moved another rung toward being human. There are multiple dimensions, and progress has been very uneven. We should celebrate these results while being precise about what they demonstrate and what remains to be understood.

r002.rationale: The response does not discuss when language emerged in the evolutionary history of intelligence.

r003.rationale: It mentions perception, action, and robot limitations, but does not state that AI must master basic sensorimotor competence to fully master intelligence.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the progress is remarkable, but we have to be careful about what we infer from it. Beating the world champion at chess or Go tells us that we can build a system that is extraordinarily good at a particular task. It doesn’t establish that the system has the breadth of human intelligence. And doing well on an examination, impressive as that is, is still one way of measuring intelligence.

I like to think about the abilities of a child. A child can move around, pick things up, learn how objects behave, and interact with people. Those abilities don’t look as spectacular as solving a difficult examination problem, but they involve an enormous amount of intelligence. We still struggle to give robots that kind of competence.

So I wouldn’t put progress on a single scale and say we are some percentage of the way to human intelligence. We have made tremendous progress in some dimensions, particularly with language. In others—perception, physical interaction, learning from relatively little experience—we have a great deal left to understand.
